author: Michael Blair
title: Apple: Caution Warranted - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) guidance for its Q1 2019 release was for a strong quarter. In its Q4 release, Apple guided as follows:
Today, the bloom came off the rose and Apple reduced its guidance by $5 to $9 billion in revenue, pointing to lower iPhone sales as the cause. It is hard to imagine a quarter where Apple falls short of its own guidance by anything like $9 billion. The market is likely to punish Apple shares if there is no offsetting positive news.
Apple’s decision to price the iPhone X north of $1,000 is a likely culprit. Only die-hard Apple fans have any interest in paying $1,000 for a phone to replace one they may have paid as little as $649 to purchase. The iPhone X starts at $999 and the X Plus at $1,149. The most recent iPhones offer little relief from the high prices and are seeing the pinch.
Competitor Samsung seems to be getting a similarly soft response to its Galaxy S9 and S9 Plus released not that long ago with reports of sales in the first month of about 8 million units.
Samsung and Huawei are strong, well-financed and highly innovative competitors to Apple for the premium smartphone segment and their determined efforts to succeed cannot be dismissed by Apple fans.
I see iPhone sales for Q2 of 50 million more or less at an average price of about $775 as the mix shifts away from the iPhone flagships. Apple has done an admirable job of raising ASP’s over the past few years, adding about $150 per device. That price increase flows through to operating profits and the price increase alone contributed over $30 billion in margin in 2017 or about half of the $61 billion operating profit Apple reported for that year. That margin is now under pressure as the high prices see volume declines.
Apple now admits margins are falling. The company says it will no longer report iPhone unit sales, a dangerous indicator that management is not confident it will see robust demand. Instead, Apple wants investors to focus on revenue from services, a segment that has been growing nicely.
Some forecasts put the iPhone installed base at more than 800 million comprising both devices purchased new and second-hand.
If the installed base is 800 million units, Apple gets about $40 per user in services revenue, and shares that with services providers on iTunes and in the App store. Services revenue per user has little room to grow in my view, and lower iPhone sales can't help. Apple’s share price discounts rapid growth in services already, at least 25% by my estimation. Recent forecasts see services revenue approaching $35 billion this year.
Apple services revenue grew 24% in 2018 and 23% in 2017, so the trend is positive. Rapid growth in services must be material to offset any significant decline in iPhone revenue. With Q1 revenue being called off at least $5 billion, growth in services will have to exceed 30% to make up the lost margin. That is unlikely. Apple’s iPhone margin is at least 60% in my opinion, and a fall of $15 billion in annual iPhone revenue cannot sensibly be made up in services revenue.
Investors should watch the details of the Q1 release when it comes out (although it may be short on details given the current thinking at Apple to refuse to publish unit sales). If services revenue growth falls short of 25%, it is time to exit the stock.
